title: 25 customer satisfaction survey questions that drive action
summary: Explore customer satisfaction survey questions that uncover friction, identify churn risk and turn customer feedback into meaningful action.
body_markdown:
Consumer satisfaction can be tricky to gauge. When a survey comes back with mostly positive scores, it’s tempting to take that as proof that customers are happy. But beneath those numbers, customers may be encountering frustrations that gradually weaken their loyalty.


The problem often comes down to the questions you ask. A customer satisfaction survey needs to do more than confirm that someone had a generally positive experience. For example, if a customer says they were satisfied after contacting support, does that mean their issue was resolved? That they were happy with the representative? Or simply that the interaction wasn’t as frustrating as they expected?


Good survey questions are designed with a purpose. They uncover what’s working, where customers are struggling and what your business can do differently to improve the experience. If you want to understand whether a customer is satisfied—and find opportunities to[increase customer loyalty](https://www.ooma.com/blog/business/increase-customer-loyalty-with-phone-surveys/) —it starts with asking the right questions.


Here are 25 questions to ask about customer satisfaction, designed to give you insights you can actually act on.


## Top questions to ask about customer satisfaction


A customer satisfaction survey, also referred to as a customer sat survey, customer feedback survey or CSAT survey questionnaire, is a structured way to collect feedback about how customers perceive their experience with your company, product or service.


While a general satisfaction rating can provide a useful benchmark, you also want to go a step further with questions that can help you understand why a customer feels the way they do and what you can do about it.


Let’s take a look at the top customer survey questions to ask, grouped by purpose.


### Questions that identify unhappy customers


#### 1. How satisfied are you with your overall \[company/product/service\] experience?


**Why ask it:** This is a straightforward way to gauge overall satisfaction and establish a baseline for your survey. It can also help you identify customers whose experience falls below your expectations.


**How to act on it:** Set a threshold for low scores and follow up with those customers. Look for patterns in the responses to understand whether dissatisfaction is concentrated around a particular product, service, customer segment or stage of the journey.


#### 2. How well does \[specific product/service\] meet your expectations?


**Why ask it:** A customer can be reasonably satisfied while still feeling that a particular product or service falls short of what they expected.


**How to act on it:** Compare responses with the expectations you set in your marketing, sales process, onboarding and product messaging. If customers consistently expect something you don’t deliver, you may need to adjust the experience or the expectations you create.


#### 3. How likely are you to continue using \[product/service\]?


**Why ask it:** This question can reveal early signs of dissatisfaction without directly asking whether a customer intends to leave.


**How to act on it:** Identify customers with low intent to continue, then follow up with them to understand what’s influencing their decision. That way, you can address recurring issues before they drive wider churn.


#### 4. How disappointed would you be if you could no longer use \[product/service\]?


**Why ask it:** This gets at how valuable your product or service is to the customer. A customer may report being satisfied but still see your offering as easily replaceable.


**How to act on it:** Follow up with questions about why a customer may have low levels of disappointment. These responses can point to missing features, weak differentiation or parts of the experience that aren’t delivering enough value.


#### 5. What could we have done differently to make your experience better?


**Why ask it:** Open-ended questions give customers a chance to highlight problems your predefined survey options may miss.


**How to act on it:** Group responses into recurring themes rather than treating every comment as an isolated complaint. Prioritize issues that appear frequently or affect important parts of the customer experience, then use future surveys to see whether changes improve satisfaction.


### Questions that uncover moments of friction


#### 6. How easy was it to \[complete a specific task or process\]?


**Why ask it:** Ease of use is often a better indicator of friction than asking whether customers are satisfied overall. A customer might like your product but find certain tasks unnecessarily complicated.


**How to act on it:** Identify the tasks or processes receiving the lowest ratings and examine where customers are getting stuck. Simplifying instructions, reducing steps or improving the user interface can remove unnecessary obstacles.


#### 7. How easy was it to find the information you needed?


**Why ask it:** This question helps reveal gaps in your content and information architecture. When customers can’t quickly find an answer, they may search your website, contact support or give up altogether.


**How to act on it:** Look for patterns in what customers say they couldn’t find. Use those insights to improve your FAQs, help center, website navigation or other customer-facing resources.


#### 8. How much effort did you have to put in to get what you needed from us?


**Why ask it:** A customer may ultimately get what they need and still have a frustrating experience getting there. Measuring perceived effort can uncover problems that a traditional satisfaction score misses.


**How to act on it:** Investigate high-effort experiences and map the steps customers take to complete them. Look for opportunities to eliminate unnecessary handoffs, forms, waiting periods or repetitive requests.


#### 9. Was there anything about your experience that was confusing or frustrating?


**Why ask it:** This open-ended question gives customers room to flag friction you might not have anticipated. It can also reveal issues that don’t fit neatly into predefined survey categories.


**How to act on it:** Look for recurring themes across responses. If customers repeatedly mention the same confusing step, policy or interaction, prioritize it as an opportunity for improvement.


### Questions that diagnose service problems


#### 10. How satisfied were you with the response time of our customer support team?


**Why ask it:** Long waits can be frustrating even when the eventual support is helpful. This question separates the quality of the response from how quickly the customer received it.


**How to act on it:** Compare this response against factors such as channel, time of day and issue type. If certain areas consistently receive poor ratings, consider adjustments to staffing, routing or response-time targets.


#### 11. Was your issue resolved to your satisfaction?


**Why ask it:** A friendly or helpful interaction that prompts them to express satisfaction in a survey doesn’t necessarily mean the customer’s problem was actually solved.


**How to act on it:** Track unresolved issues and look for common reasons they remain open. If customers frequently need multiple contacts to resolve the same type of problem, investigate whether your team needs better tools, training or escalation paths.


#### 12. How satisfied were you with the knowledge and helpfulness of the support representative?


**Why ask it:** This question helps distinguish an issue with the service process from an issue with the interaction itself.


**How to act on it:** Analyze low scores alongside the types of issues customers were contacting you about. Recurring gaps may point to opportunities for better training, documentation or access to information on those particular issues.


#### 13. How well did our customer support team understand your needs?


**Why ask it:** Customers don’t want to repeatedly explain their situation or receive generic answers. This question can reveal whether your support experience feels personalized and relevant.


**How to act on it:** Improving customer history visibility, internal notes and communication between teams can help create a more connected support experience.


### Questions that reveal what to improve


#### 14. What is the one thing we could improve about your experience with \[company/product\]?


**Why ask it:** Asking customers to identify just one improvement encourages them to focus on what matters most rather than producing a long list of minor suggestions.


**How to act on it:** Organize responses by theme and look for suggestions that come up repeatedly. Prioritize changes based on how frequently they’re mentioned, how much they affect the customer experience and how feasible they are to implement.


#### 15. Which part of your experience with \[company/product\] would you most like to see improved?


**Why ask it:** Customers interact with your business across multiple touchpoints. This question helps identify which part of the overall experience has the most room for improvement.


**How to act on it:** Compare responses across customer segments and touchpoints. If one area consistently stands out, investigate the underlying causes and assign ownership for improving it.


#### 16. What could we do to make your experience with \[company/product\] easier?


**Why ask it:** This question puts the focus on reducing effort rather than simply increasing satisfaction. Customers may be able to identify small changes that would make a meaningful difference to their experience.


**How to act on it:** Start with suggestions around small changes that can quickly eliminate recurring sources of frustration before tackling popular suggestions that will take more time to implement.


#### 17. Is there anything you expected from us that you didn’t receive?


**Why ask it:** This can uncover gaps between customer expectations and what your business actually delivers. Those gaps may involve features, service, communication or the overall experience.


**How to act on it:** Separate responses into issues that require changes to the product or service and those that reflect an expectation-setting problem. You may need to improve the experience, clarify your offering or both.


### Questions that identify loyalty or churn risk


#### 18. How likely are you to recommend \[company/product\] to a friend or colleague?


**Why ask it:** This provides a useful indicator of customer loyalty. Customers who are willing to recommend you generally demonstrate a more loyal relationship than those who are merely satisfied.


**How to act on it:** Track responses over time and segment them by customer type, product or experience. Follow up with low scorers to understand what’s holding them back and with high scorers to learn what they value most.


#### 19. How likely are you to switch to another provider in the next \[six months/year\]?


**Why ask it:** This question addresses churn risk directly and can help identify customers who may be considering alternatives even if they haven’t complained or given a particularly low satisfaction score.


**How to act on it:** Flag high-risk responses for further analysis or proactive outreach. Look for common reasons customers are considering switching and address those issues before they become actual churn.


#### 20. How well does \[company/product\] compare with alternatives you’re considering?


**Why ask it:** A customer may be happy enough with your business while still believing a competitor offers better value, features, service or convenience.


**How to act on it:** Analyze what customers say competitors do better. Use those insights to inform product development, pricing, service improvements or how you communicate your competitive advantages.


#### 21. How much value do you feel you’re getting from \[product/service\]?


**Why ask it:** Customers can be satisfied with an experience while questioning whether it’s worth the money, time or effort. Perceived value is therefore an important part of understanding whether a relationship is likely to last.


**How to act on it:** If customers consistently see your product or service as low value, investigate whether the problem is the offering itself, how customers use it or whether its benefits are being communicated effectively.


### Questions that reveal growth areas


#### 22. What additional products, services or features would you like to see from us?


**Why ask it:** Customers can point to needs that your current offering doesn’t address, highlighting opportunities for new features, complementary services or new products.


**How to act on it:** Group similar suggestions, looking for requests that appear consistently. Validate promising ideas with additional research before investing further.


#### 23. Is there anything you currently use another provider for that you’d like us to offer?


**Why ask it:** This question reveals opportunities to solve more of a customer’s needs within your existing relationship. It can also show where competitors may be pulling customers away.


**How to act on it:** If demand for a particular capability is strong, evaluate whether adding it to your offering could increase retention, adoption or customer value.


#### 24. Are there any other ways you would like to use our product or service?


**Why ask it:** Customers sometimes find valuable use cases that a business didn’t originally anticipate. Their answers can reveal new applications, customer segments or ways to expand adoption.


**How to act on it:** Share recurring use cases with product, marketing and sales teams. These answers could inform new features, educational content, positioning or opportunities to introduce existing capabilities to more customers.


#### 25. Is there anything else you’d like to share or suggest to help us improve?


**Why ask it:** An open-ended question gives customers the final word and creates space for feedback that your other questions didn’t capture. Some of the most useful insights may come from something you didn’t think to ask about.


**How to act on it:** Don’t let these responses disappear into a spreadsheet. Categorize recurring suggestions, share relevant feedback to the appropriate teams and look for themes that can inform future improvements and customer experience initiatives.


## How to quantify consumer satisfaction


The sample customer service survey questions above can help you understand what customers think and why. To track performance over time, you can also turn some of those responses into a measurable score. Three common approaches are CSAT, NPS and the customer satisfaction index.


**[Customer satisfaction score](https://www.ooma.com/blog/business/what-customer-satisfaction-score-is-telling-you/) (CSAT)** measures how satisfied customers are with a specific interaction, product or experience. Customers typically rate their satisfaction on a scale, such as 1–5. To calculate CSAT, divide the number of satisfied responses by the total number of responses and multiply by 100. For example, if 80 out of 100 responses indicate a positive rating, your CSAT is 80 percent.


**Net Promoter Score (NPS)** measures loyalty by asking how likely customers are to recommend your business on a 0–10 scale. Subtract the percentage of detractors (0–6) from the percentage of promoters (9–10), leaving passives (7–8) out of the calculation. An NPS can range from -100 to +100.


**Customer satisfaction index (CSI)** takes a broader view by combining responses to multiple satisfaction questions. There isn’t one universal CSI formula, so businesses typically calculate an average or weighted score across selected questions. This provides a broader benchmark for overall satisfaction while the individual responses show where improvements are needed.


## Acting on your customer satisfaction survey results


Client satisfaction surveys can be conducted in many ways, from online forms and email surveys to phone calls and in-person conversations. Whatever format you choose, the goal is the same: **ask questions that give you useful insight into the customer experience and what you can do to improve it.** If you’re conducting a client feedback survey by phone, good[business phone etiquette](https://www.ooma.com/blog/business/business-communications-phone-etiquette/) can also help ensure the survey itself is a positive customer interaction.


Most importantly, don’t let the responses stop at a score. Use what customers tell you to address problems and find new opportunities to improve. With the right customer satisfaction questions, you can turn customer feedback into meaningful action and build experiences that keep your customers coming back.
